warmup.q: Three helper coroutines each run for (dish in hatch) serve(dish) over the same Channel<String>. The cook sends 9 dishes into it, then closes it. How many times is each dish served?
options: Three times: every helper gets every dish
Exactly once: each element goes to one receiver
Once, but all 9 go to whichever helper started first
It can't work: only one coroutine may receive from a channel
warmup.why: A channel is a queue: each element is received by exactly one receiver, like a plate taken off the hatch. Several receivers on one channel is fan-out, and the channel serves waiting receivers in turn, so the dishes spread across the three helpers. Sending every value to every subscriber is what a SharedFlow does, the bell from the last lesson.

opening:
Between the kitchen and the dining room of an old house there's a hatch, a small window in the wall with a shelf. The cook puts a plate on the shelf, and on the other side a helper picks it up and carries it to the table. The shelf holds two plates. When it's full, the cook waits. When it's empty, the helper waits. And a plate, unlike a ring of the bell, can be eaten only once.

StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams ended at this hatch. Its board and bell sent every value to everyone. A queue between coroutines, a line of items taken out in the order they went in, hands each item to exactly one taker, and that's how work gets shared out. The easy trap is the last plate. The helper can't see the cook take off her apron, and unless she tells him, he waits at the hatch all night.

In this lesson, we'll build the hatch and size its shelf, put a team of helpers behind it, take whichever answer comes first, and find the hatches hidden inside flows. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at a hatch between the kitchen and the dining room, with a shelf for two plates. A channel is that hatch: each element goes to one receiver, the capacity sets the pace, and close() is the cook's word that the last plate is through. A team of helpers on one hatch caps the work, select takes whichever answer comes first, and callbackFlow hides a hatch inside a flow.

Now search your own code for Channel(. For each channel, find the line that closes it, and ask how full its shelf may get.

Next, we'll hang one shopping list on the fridge for every helper to write on. What happens when coroutines share a variable instead of passing plates?

sections.h: A channel is the hatch between coroutines, and its shelf sets the pace
sections.html:
A Channel<T> connects coroutines, pieces of work that can pause without holding a thread, the worker that runs the code. One coroutine calls send to put an element in, and another calls receive to take one out. Each element is received exactly once, by one receiver. That's the difference from the SharedFlow of the last lesson, where every subscriber heard every ring.

Java
// Java equivalent: a bounded BlockingQueue, with an end marker because a queue can't be closed
BlockingQueue<String> hatch = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2);
Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
    for (String dish : dinner) putQuietly(hatch, dish);   // blocks while the queue is full
    putQuietly(hatch, LAST);
});
for (String dish = hatch.take(); !dish.equals(LAST); dish = hatch.take()) serve(dish);
Kotlin
val hatch = Channel<String>(capacity = 2)
launch {
    for (dish in dinner) hatch.send(dish)   // suspends while the shelf is full
    hatch.close()                           // the last plate: the receiving loop will end
}
for (dish in hatch) serve(dish)              // receives until the hatch is closed and empty

Read the Kotlin aloud: the cook puts each dish through the hatch, then says "that's the last one", and the helper serves plates until the hatch is closed and empty. The Java version is the BlockingQueue from the first track, with one difference that matters. Where a queue blocks a thread, a channel suspends a coroutine, so a helper waiting at an empty hatch holds no thread at all.

The capacity is the size of the shelf: how many elements can wait in the channel before send has to suspend. The default, a rendezvous channel, has no shelf at all. The cook holds the plate until a helper's hands take it.

Capacity send suspends when Picture it Like
Channel.RENDEZVOUS (0, the default) no receiver is waiting no shelf: hand to hand SynchronousQueue
Channel(n) n elements are already waiting a shelf with n spots ArrayBlockingQueue(n)
Channel.BUFFERED 64 are waiting (a JVM property changes the default) a long shelf ArrayBlockingQueue(64)
Channel.UNLIMITED never: memory is the limit a shelf with no end LinkedBlockingQueue
Channel.CONFLATED never: a new element replaces the waiting one one spot, and the new plate takes it no JDK equivalent

Predict the four lines before you read them. ChannelCapacities, in the Try it below, has a cook who puts five plates through the hatch as fast as she can, and a helper who needs 100 ms per plate:

RENDEZVOUS   send() returned at [38, 142, 247, 348, 448] ms received [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
capacity 2   send() returned at [0, 0, 0, 101, 201] ms     received [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
UNLIMITED    send() returned at [0, 0, 0, 0, 0] ms         received [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
CONFLATED    send() returned at [3, 3, 3, 3, 3] ms         received [1, 5]

With no shelf, the cook moved in step with the helper, one plate every 100 ms (the first 38 ms is the program warming up). With a shelf for two, three sends returned at once: two plates on the shelf, and one straight into the helper's hands. Then the cook waited. UNLIMITED never waited. CONFLATED never waited either, and only plates 1 and 5 were received, because each new plate replaced the one on the shelf.

That waiting has a name. Backpressure is a slow receiver slowing down a fast sender, so work doesn't pile up between them. A rendezvous channel gives it for free, which is why it's the default. Add a small shelf to absorb bursts. Be suspicious of UNLIMITED: with a slow helper, plates pile up until the program runs out of memory, an OutOfMemoryError some hours later.

Now the last plate. for (dish in hatch) ends only when the channel is closed and empty. Delete hatch.close() in the Try it, and the program never ends. The helper waits at the hatch, loyal to a fault, for a plate that will never come. Here the picture breaks: a real helper would see the cook take off her apron. A coroutine can't tell "later" from "never" until someone calls close().

The produce { } builder does it for you. It starts a coroutine that sends into a new channel, closes the channel when the block ends or fails, and returns its receiving half, a ReceiveChannel. It is still marked @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi in kotlinx.coroutines 1.11, so it needs an opt-in.

A receiver stops only when the channel is closed. Close it, or let produce close it.

A channel is hot, like the board and the bell: plates sit on the shelf whether or not anyone takes them, and a coroutine suspended in send waits until someone does. For a stream with one consumer, a cold Flow, the recipe card of Flow basics that runs only when someone collects it, is usually simpler. Channels earn their place when coroutines hand work to each other, and the first job worth handing out is more dishes than one helper can carry.

code.title: ChannelCapacities.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l09 import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** The cook puts 5 plates through the hatch as fast as she can; the helper needs 100 ms per plate. */ suspend fun run(label: String, hatch: Channel<Int>) = coroutineScope { val t0 = System.nanoTime() fun ms() = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val sendTimes = mutableListOf<Long>() launch { for (plate in 1..5) { hatch.send(plate); sendTimes += ms() } hatch.close() // no more plates: the helper's for loop ends after the last one } val received = mutableListOf<Int>() for (plate in hatch) { delay(100); received += plate } println("%-12s send() returned at %-26s received %s".format(label, sendTimes.toString() + " ms", received)) } fun main() = runBlocking { run("RENDEZVOUS", Channel(Channel.RENDEZVOUS)) run("capacity 2", Channel(2)) run("UNLIMITED", Channel(Channel.UNLIMITED)) run("CONFLATED", Channel(Channel.CONFLATED)) }

alt.title: ChannelCapacitiesJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of ChannelCapacities.kt: blocking queues between two threads. SynchronousQueue // is a rendezvous, ArrayBlockingQueue(2) has capacity 2, LinkedBlockingQueue is unbounded. // The JDK has no conflated queue; Kotlin's CONFLATED channel keeps only the newest element. // A blocking queue has no close(), so the cook sends a marker (-1) at the end instead. package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue; public class ChannelCapacitiesJava { static void run(String label, BlockingQueue<Integer> hatch) throws InterruptedException { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<Long> sendTimes = new ArrayList<>(); Thread cook = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { try { for (int plate = 1; plate <= 5; plate++) { hatch.put(plate); sendTimes.add((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } hatch.put(-1); // the end marker } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); List<Integer> received = new ArrayList<>(); for (int plate = hatch.take(); plate != -1; plate = hatch.take()) { Thread.sleep(100); received.add(plate); } cook.join(); System.out.printf("%-22s put() returned at %-26s received %s%n", label, sendTimes + " ms", received); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("SynchronousQueue", new SynchronousQueue<>()); run("ArrayBlockingQueue(2)", new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2)); run("LinkedBlockingQueue", new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()); } }

try.expect: Rendezvous: each send returns about 100 ms after the previous one, in step with the helper. Capacity 2: the first three return at once (two on the shelf, one handed straight to the waiting helper), then one every 100 ms. Unlimited: all five at once. Conflated: all five at once, but only [1, 5] is received, because each new plate replaced the waiting one. Without close(), the program never ends: the for loop waits for a plate that will never come (stop it with Ctrl+C). The Java twin's three queues match the first three lines.

sections.h: Fan out to a team of helpers, and fan in to one table
sections.html:
One helper at the hatch carries one plate at a time. Twenty dishes of about 100 ms each take two seconds. The fix in a real kitchen is plain: put more helpers at the same hatch.

That's fan-out: several coroutines receive from the same channel. Each element still goes to exactly one of them, and channels are fair: receivers waiting in line are served in the order they asked. So one channel plus N helper coroutines is a team that cooks at most N dishes at once, with no thread pool involved. Fan-in is the reverse: many senders into one channel, read by one receiver, like every helper bringing finished plates to one table.

Here is the lab's cookAll, which cooks a list of dishes with a fixed number of helpers and returns what each dish became:

Java
// Java equivalent: a fixed pool takes tasks from its queue, a CompletionService collects results
Map<String, String> cookAll(List<String> dishes, int helpers) throws Exception {
    try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(helpers)) {
        CompletionService<Map.Entry<String, String>> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool);
        for (String dish : dishes) done.submit(() -> Map.entry(dish, cook(dish)));
        Map<String, String> result = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < dishes.size(); i++) { var e = done.take().get(); result.put(e.getKey(), e.getValue()); }
        return result;
    }
}
Kotlin
suspend fun cookAll(dishes: List<String>, helpers: Int, cook: suspend (String) -> String): Map<String, String> =
    coroutineScope {
        val hatch = produce { dishes.forEach { send(it) } }        // fan-out source
        val done = Channel<Pair<String, String>>()                 // fan-in
        val team = List(helpers) { launch { for (dish in hatch) done.send(dish to cook(dish)) } }
        launch { team.joinAll(); done.close() }                    // close once every helper is done
        val result = mutableMapOf<String, String>()
        for ((dish, plate) in done) result[dish] = plate
        result
    }

Walk through it in order. produce puts the dishes through a rendezvous hatch, one at a time. List(helpers) { launch { ... } } starts the team. Each helper loops over the hatch, cooks what it gets and sends the result into done. A separate coroutine waits for the whole team with joinAll(), then closes done. Finally, the caller's loop reads done into a map.

The tricky line is the closer. Close done too early, and a helper's send throws ClosedSendChannelException. Never close it, and the caller's loop waits all night, like the helper in the last section. A coroutine of its own that calls joinAll() and then close() is the usual answer.

FanOutFanIn, in the Try it below, runs the same shape with 20 dishes of 50 to 150 ms each:

4 helpers: {helper 0=5, helper 1=4, helper 2=6, helper 3=5}
20 dishes took 614 ms

Twenty dishes of about 100 ms on four helpers should take about 500 ms, and 614 is close on a busy machine. With -Pargs=1 the same run took 2,181 ms, and with -Pargs=10 it took 324 ms, two dishes per helper.

Everything sits inside coroutineScope, so the pipeline belongs to its caller's job tree, as in Structured concurrency. If one cook throws, the scope cancels the producer, the other helpers and the closer, then rethrows. No coroutine is left waiting at a hatch.

Why not dishes.map { async { cook(it) } }.awaitAll()? Because that starts every call at once. Order 5,000 loaves that way, and the bakery gets 5,000 phone calls in the same second, and it will not thank you. The team caps them at N. It also gives each helper a natural home for its own things, such as one pan per helper. And it grows into a pipeline: stations in a row with a channel between each pair, such as shape, then bake, then pack, each with as many helpers as it needs. The worked example below builds one.

A fixed team on one channel caps the work at the team's size. Size the team to what the slow part can take.

A team takes whatever comes through the hatch next. Sometimes, though, you are waiting for two different things, and you want whichever comes first.

code.title: FanOutFanIn.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l09 import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.produce import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.joinAll import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.random.Random @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val helpers = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 4 val t0 = System.nanoTime() coroutineScope { // 1. one cook puts 20 dishes through the hatch, one at a time val hatch = produce { for (i in 1..20) send("dish-$i") } // 2. fan-out: each dish goes to exactly one helper val table = Channel<String>() val team = List(helpers) { h -> launch { for (dish in hatch) { delay(Random.nextLong(50, 150)) // carrying it, serving it table.send("$dish by helper $h") } } } // 3. fan-in: close the table channel when every helper is done launch { team.joinAll(); table.close() } val perHelper = mutableMapOf<String, Int>() for (served in table) perHelper.merge(served.substringAfter("by "), 1, Int::plus) println("$helpers helpers: ${perHelper.toSortedMap()}") } println("20 dishes took ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") }

alt.title: FanOutFanInJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of FanOutFanIn.kt: a fixed pool takes tasks from its queue (fan-out), and an // ExecutorCompletionService hands back results in the order they finish (fan-in). package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorCompletionService; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom; public class FanOutFanInJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int helpers = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 4; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(helpers)) { ExecutorCompletionService<String> table = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool); for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) { String dish = "dish-" + i; table.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(50, 150)); // carrying it, serving it return dish + " by " + Thread.currentThread().getName(); }); } Map<String, Integer> perHelper = new TreeMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) perHelper.merge(table.take().get().split(" by ")[1], 1, Integer::sum); System.out.println(helpers + " helpers: " + perHelper); } System.out.println("20 dishes took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); } }

With 10 helpers it takes about 300 ms, and each helper serves about 2. The Java twin spreads the work across its four pool threads the same way.

sections.h: Take whichever answer comes first with select
sections.html:
Picture the cook phoning two bakeries to ask who still has bread tonight. The corner bakery takes 300 ms to answer, and the market bakery 120 ms. She'll take the first answer and hang up on the other. If neither answers within 500 ms, she'll bake her own.

select { } is that pair of phone calls. It suspends until the first of several clauses, the things it waits on, can complete. Then it runs that clause and drops the rest. The clauses you'll use are deferred.onAwait (an async result is ready), channel.onReceive (a plate is at the hatch), channel.onSend(value) (there's room on the shelf) and onTimeout(ms), the kitchen timer.

Java
// Java equivalent: anyOf completes with the first future, completeOnTimeout adds a fallback
Object first = CompletableFuture.anyOf(corner, market)
    .completeOnTimeout("we bake our own", 500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    .join();
corner.cancel(true); market.cancel(true);     // only marks the futures; the calls may run on
Kotlin
val answer = coroutineScope {
    val corner = async { cornerBakery.ask() }
    val market = async { marketBakery.ask() }
    val first = select {
        corner.onAwait { it }
        market.onAwait { it }
        onTimeout(500) { "we bake our own" }   // needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
    }
    corner.cancel(); market.cancel()          // hang up on the others
    first
}

Expect the market's answer after about 120 ms. SelectFirst, in the Try it below, printed this:

after 213 ms: market bakery: plenty of sourdough

The extra 90 ms is a cold program on a busy machine: the clock starts before the coroutine machinery has loaded. With -Pargs=100, a budget of 100 ms, the timer won: nobody answered within 100 ms: we bake our own bread.

Three details matter. First, select is biased: if several clauses are ready at the same moment, the first one listed wins, so list the one you prefer first. Second, hanging up is your job, just as with anyOf. The difference is what the hang-up reaches. A coroutine's cancel arrives at the losing call's next suspension point, as Cancellation and timeouts showed. future.cancel(true) only marks a Java future as cancelled, and the work behind it may run on. Third, the status is mixed. In 1.11 the select builder compiles without an opt-in, the guide still calls select expressions experimental, and onTimeout needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class).

Without the timer, this is the lab's firstOffer, written for a list of shops: select { calls.forEach { c -> c.onAwait { it } } }. The lambda registers one clause per call.

select over the onReceive clauses of several channels can merge streams by hand, like a helper at two hatches, one for soup and one for bread, who takes whichever plate shows up first. For most merging, though, Flow operators such as merge and combine are simpler and harder to get wrong. Keep select for "the first of these, then stop", and for the rare loop that must react to whichever of several channels has something.

select takes the first clause that's ready, and prefers the first one listed. Cancel the losers yourself.

Every channel so far was one we made on purpose. The last two hide inside flows, and one of them rescues an old gadget.

Cancelling the losers is up to you. package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class SelectFirstJava { static String answer(String text, long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return text; } public static void main(String[] args) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long budgetMs = args.length > 0 ? With 100 ms the timer wins: nobody answered within 100 ms: we bake our own bread. The Java twin gives the same answers with anyOf and completeOnTimeout.

sections.h: Hatches inside flows: callbackFlow and the backpressure operators
sections.html:
A flow is sequential: emit may be called only from the flow's own coroutine, as Flow basics showed. Some values come from somewhere else. Picture an older wireless oven probe, a thermometer you push into the roast. Its library has a listener API: you register a function, and the probe calls it on its own thread with every new reading, until you unregister it. Such a function is a callback, code you hand over for someone else to call later.

callbackFlow turns that into a Flow by putting a channel inside it. The callback calls trySend on the channel, and the collector receives from it:

Java
// Java equivalent: Flux.create with a sink, and onDispose for the cleanup
Flux<Reading> readings(OvenProbe probe) {
    return Flux.create(sink -> {
        Registration registration = probe.register(sink::next);
        sink.onDispose(registration::unregister);
    });
}
Kotlin
fun OvenProbe.readings(): Flow<Reading> = callbackFlow {
    val registration = register { reading -> trySend(reading) }   // called on the probe's thread
    awaitClose { registration.unregister() }                      // runs when the collector stops
}

awaitClose is not optional. It suspends until the collector goes away, then runs the cleanup. Without it, the block returns right after registering, and callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException rather than leave the listener behind. That's the bug in the lab's starting code. From the callback, use trySend: it never blocks the probe's thread, and it fails if the channel's buffer (64 by default) is full. For a callback that fires once, suspendCancellableCoroutine from Suspend functions from zero is the right tool. And channelFlow is the same idea for your own coroutines: launch several producers inside it, and each one can send safely.

The other hidden channels sit inside three backpressure operators. Take the guide's numbers, told with our probe: a reading every 100 ms, a screen on the fridge that needs 300 ms to redraw, and three readings. FlowBackpressure, in the Try it below, measured them:

Pipeline The screen shows Expected Measured here
plain 1, 2, 3 1,200 ms: (100 + 300) x 3 1,246 ms
buffer() 1, 2, 3 1,000 ms: the probe runs ahead 1,061 ms
conflate() 1, 3 700 ms: a busy screen skips to the latest 720 ms
collectLatest { } starts 1, 2 and 3, finishes only 3 600 ms: a new reading cancels the old work 619 ms

buffer keeps every reading and lets the probe run ahead into a channel. conflate keeps only the latest, which suits a thermometer and never suits a list of orders. collectLatest cancels and restarts the collector's block for each new value, like a cook who starts the sauce again every time someone changes their order. That suits "work out the time left whenever the temperature changes". It's wrong for anything with side effects you can't take back, because the cancelled run may have done half its work.

All three trade memory, completeness and freshness against each other, and the plain flow is the safe default. Reactor makes the same three trades with onBackpressureBuffer, onBackpressureLatest and switchMap, as Backpressure in practice showed in the reactive track, and the Java twin measures them.

Pick buffer, conflate or collectLatest by asking which values you can afford to lose.

Every hatch in this lesson moved a plate from one coroutine to another, so no two coroutines ever held the same plate. A kitchen also has things that everyone writes on.

try.title: Time four ways to keep up
steps: Read FlowBackpressure.kt. Predict what each of the four lines prints, and roughly how long it takes.
Run it.
In the conflate() line, change the collector's delay(300) to delay(50). Predict first: does it still skip a reading?
Run the Java twin with the Reactor counterparts.

code.title: FlowBackpressure.kt
code.html: package workbench.coroutines.l09 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.buffer import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.collectLatest import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.conflate import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** Three readings from the oven probe, 100 ms apart. */ fun ovenReadings(): Flow<Int> = flow { for (i in 1..3) { delay(100); emit(i) } } fun main() = runBlocking { // the collector takes 300 ms per reading (redrawing the screen on the fridge) val plain = measureTimeMillis { ovenReadings().collect { delay(300); print("$it ") } } println(" plain: $plain ms") val buffered = measureTimeMillis { ovenReadings().buffer().collect { delay(300); print("$it ") } } println(" buffer(): $buffered ms") val conflated = measureTimeMillis { ovenReadings().conflate().collect { delay(300); print("$it ") } } println(" conflate(): $conflated ms") val latest = measureTimeMillis { ovenReadings().collectLatest { print("start $it, "); delay(300); print("done $it ") } } println(" collectLatest: $latest ms") }

alt.title: FlowBackpressureJava.java
alt.html: // Java equivalent of FlowBackpressure.kt with Reactor: concatMap with prefetch 0 (ask for the // next reading only when the screen has drawn the last one) is close to a plain flow, // onBackpressureBuffer to buffer(), onBackpressureLatest to conflate(), and switchMap to // collectLatest (a new reading cancels the work on the previous one). package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.function.Function; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class FlowBackpressureJava { /** Three readings from the oven probe, 100 ms apart, produced only when asked for (like a cold flow). */ static Flux<Integer> readings() { return Flux.range(1, 3).concatMap(i -> Mono.just(i).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(100)), 1); } /** Redrawing the screen on the fridge: 300 ms per reading. */ static Mono<Integer> draw(int i) { return Mono.just(i).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(300)).doOnNext(x -> System.out.print(x + " ")); } static void time(String label, Function<Flux<Integer>, Flux<Integer>> pipeline) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); pipeline.apply(readings()).blockLast(); System.out.printf(" %-26s %d ms%n", label, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } public static void main(String[] args) { time("concatMap, prefetch 0:", f -> f.concatMap(FlowBackpressureJava::draw, 0)); time("onBackpressureBuffer:", f -> f.onBackpressureBuffer().concatMap(FlowBackpressureJava::draw, 0)); time("onBackpressureLatest:", f -> f.onBackpressureLatest().concatMap(FlowBackpressureJava::draw, 0)); time("switchMap:", f -> f.switchMap(FlowBackpressureJava::draw)); } }

try.expect: Plain: 1 2 3 in about 1,200 ms. buffer(): 1 2 3 in about 1,000 ms. conflate(): 1 3 in about 700 ms. collectLatest: start 1, start 2, start 3, done 3 in about 600 ms. With a 50 ms collector, conflate() prints 1 2 3: it skips only values that arrive while the collector is busy, and now it never is. The Java twin prints the same readings in about the same times with concatMap, onBackpressureBuffer, onBackpressureLatest and switchMap.

compare.title: A capped team of helpers: ExecutorService vs a channel and coroutines

java.title: BreadRun.java
java.html: List<String> orderAll(List<String> loaves) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) { // 1. 8 threads = at most 8 calls CompletionService<String> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool); for (String loaf : loaves) done.submit(() -> bakery.order(loaf)); // 2. every task queued up front List<String> tickets = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < loaves.size(); i++) tickets.add(done.take().get()); // 3. fan-in, in finish order return tickets; } // a failure surfaces at get(); the other tasks keep running until close() waits for them }

kotlin.title: BreadRun.kt
kotlin.html: suspend fun orderAll(loaves: List<String>): List<String> = coroutineScope { val hatch = produce { loaves.forEach { send(it) } } // 2. handed out one at a time val tickets = Channel<String>() val team = List(8) { launch { for (loaf in hatch) tickets.send(bakery.order(loaf)) } } // 1. 8 helpers launch { team.joinAll(); tickets.close() } val result = mutableListOf<String>() for (t in tickets) result += t // 3. fan-in, in finish order result } // a failure cancels the producer and every helper, then rethrows

compare.note: Both keep the bakery's phone line at 8 calls at once and collect the tickets in the order the calls finish. The Java version spends 8 threads, which sit blocked while the bakery answers, and it queues every task up front. The Kotlin version spends 8 coroutines, which suspend while waiting, and the rendezvous channel hands out an order only when a helper is free, so a list of a million loaves never sits in a task queue. The bigger difference is failure. In Java, one failed order shows up at get(), and the other tasks keep running until close() waits for them. In Kotlin, the whole team is one coroutineScope, so the first failure cancels the producer and every helper before the exception reaches the caller.

steps.say: The house is baking 600 cookies for a school bake sale. Each one is shaped from the dough (quick), baked (the slow part: 20 ms per cookie in our code, and the oven holds 12 at once), and packed into boxes of 12. In one loop, the oven bakes one cookie at a time: 600 x 20 ms is 12 seconds, with 11 spots in the oven empty the whole time.
steps.code: suspend fun bakeSale(dough: Dough) { val box = mutableListOf<Cookie>() repeat(600) { val ball = dough.shape() // quick val cookie = oven.bake(ball) // 20 ms, one cookie at a time box += cookie if (box.size == 12) { packer.pack(box.toList()); box.clear() } } if (box.isNotEmpty()) packer.pack(box) }

alt.html: // Java equivalent of the same single loop void bakeSale(Dough dough) { List<Cookie> box = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 600; i++) { Ball ball = dough.shape(); // quick Cookie cookie = oven.bake(ball); // 20 ms, one cookie at a time box.add(cookie); if (box.size() == 12) { packer.pack(List.copyOf(box)); box.clear(); } } if (!box.isEmpty()) packer.pack(box); }

steps.say: Station 1 shapes the dough into a small buffer, a little ahead of the oven. produce closes the channel when the dough runs out.
steps.code: @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) suspend fun bakeSale(dough: Dough) = coroutineScope { // 1. shape: one helper, a little ahead of the oven val balls = produce(capacity = 24) { repeat(600) { send(dough.shape()) } }

alt.html: void bakeSale(Dough dough) throws Exception { // 1. shape: one thread, a little ahead of the oven BlockingQueue<Ball> balls = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(24); Thread shaper = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 600; i++) putQuietly(balls, dough.shape()); putQuietly(balls, Ball.LAST); });

steps.say: Station 2 fans out to 12 bakers, one per spot in the oven. They fan in to one channel, which a coroutine of its own closes when all 12 are done.
steps.code: // 2. bake: 12 helpers, because the oven holds 12 cookies at once val cookies = Channel<Cookie>(capacity = 48) val bakers = List(12) { launch { for (ball in balls) cookies.send(oven.bake(ball)) } } launch { bakers.joinAll(); cookies.close() }

alt.html: // 2. bake: 12 threads, because the oven holds 12 cookies at once BlockingQueue<Cookie> cookies = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(48); ExecutorService bakers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(12); for (int i = 0; i < 12; i++) bakers.submit(() -> { for (Ball ball = balls.take(); ball != Ball.LAST; ball = balls.take()) cookies.put(oven.bake(ball)); balls.put(Ball.LAST); // pass the end marker on to the next baker return null; });

steps.say: Station 3 is a single packer, so the boxes stay simple. When cookies is closed and empty, the loop ends, and coroutineScope returns once every station has finished. If any station throws, the scope cancels the others. The oven is now full: 600 x 20 ms / 12 is about one second instead of twelve.
steps.code: // 3. pack: one helper, boxes of 12 val box = mutableListOf<Cookie>() for (c in cookies) { box += c if (box.size == 12) { packer.pack(box.toList()); box.clear() } } if (box.isNotEmpty()) packer.pack(box) }

alt.html: // 3. pack: one thread, boxes of 12 (the end of station 2 needs its own marker or a latch) bakers.shutdown(); List<Cookie> box = new ArrayList<>(); while (!(bakers.isTerminated() && cookies.isEmpty())) { Cookie c = cookies.poll(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); if (c == null) continue; box.add(c); if (box.size() == 12) { packer.pack(List.copyOf(box)); box.clear(); } } if (!box.isEmpty()) packer.pack(box); shaper.join(); }

steps.say: Self-check: the packer runs out of boxes and slows to a crawl. Trace what happens to the counter and the oven. (The packer falls behind, cookies fills up to 48, the bakers suspend in send, balls fills up to 24, and the shaper suspends too. Dough never piles up on the counter, and the oven simply waits. Backpressure travels all the way back to the first station.)

lab.title: A team of helpers, an oven probe and the first shop to answer
steps: Meet the code. PipelineModel.kt has the oven probe with its listener API, the Registration it hands back, and a shop's Offer. cookAll cooks a list of dishes, but one at a time; readings() should turn the probe into a Flow; firstOffer should phone every shop and keep the first answer. Run the tests: five of seven fail.

In CookAll.kt, build the team inside coroutineScope: produce the dishes, start helpers coroutines that loop over that channel and send dish to cook(dish) into a second channel, close the second channel after joinAll(), and read it into a map.
In ProbeFlow.kt, keep the Registration that register returns, and end the block with awaitClose { registration.unregister() }.
In FirstOffer.kt, start every call with async, select on their onAwait clauses, cancel all the calls, and return the winner.
Run the tests until all seven pass.
hints: produce needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) on the function. It closes its channel when its block ends.
Close the second channel from a coroutine of its own: launch { team.joinAll(); done.close() }. If you close it after the receiving loop, the loop never ends.
awaitClose comes from kotlinx.coroutines.channels. It suspends until the collector stops, so it must be the last line of the callbackFlow block.
select { calls.forEach { c -> c.onAwait { it } } } is a whole select: the lambda registers one clause per call. Cancelling a call that already finished does nothing, so you can cancel them all.

drill.title: Three sinks, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. The kitchen has three sinks. Write suspend fun washAll(pans: List<String>) that calls the suspend function wash(pan) for every pan, with at most 3 washes at once, using a channel and 3 helper coroutines. It returns when every pan is clean, and a failure in any wash cancels the rest.

answer.html: @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) suspend fun washAll(pans: List<String>) = coroutineScope { val pile = produce { for (pan in pans) send(pan) } // closed when the block ends repeat(3) { launch { for (pan in pile) wash(pan) } // each pan goes to one helper } } // coroutineScope waits for the producer and all three helpers

alt.title: Java equivalent
alt.html: // Java equivalent: a pool of 3 threads, and invokeAll to wait for every task void washAll(List<String> pans) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService sinks = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { List<Callable<Void>> tasks = pans.stream() .<Callable<Void>>map(pan -> () -> { wash(pan); return null; }) .toList(); for (Future<Void> f : sinks.invokeAll(tasks)) f.get(); // rethrows the first failure } // unlike coroutineScope, the other washes are not cancelled on a failure }

recap: A Channel is a hatch between coroutines: each element goes to exactly one receiver, and send and receive suspend instead of blocking a thread.

Capacity is the shelf: rendezvous (the default) hands over directly, Channel(n) holds n, UNLIMITED never makes the sender wait and can run out of memory, CONFLATED keeps only the newest. Close the channel when sending is done, or let produce { } close it.
Fan-out, N coroutines on one channel, caps the work at N. Close a fan-in channel after joinAll(). Inside coroutineScope, one failure cancels the whole pipeline.
select takes whichever clause completes first (onAwait, onReceive, onTimeout). It prefers the first clause listed, and cancelling the losers is your job.
callbackFlow turns a listener into a Flow and must end with awaitClose { unregister() }. buffer, conflate and collectLatest trade completeness for speed or freshness.
The limit: a channel hands each element from one coroutine to another. It does nothing for two coroutines that change the same variable.

explain.prompt: A friend wants to order 5,000 loaves for a festival with loaves.map { async { bakery.order(it) } }.awaitAll(), and the bakery's phone line takes 8 calls at once. Explain the problem, and how a channel and a team of helpers fix it.
explain.answer: That code starts 5,000 coroutines at once, so the bakery gets 5,000 calls in the same moment, far more than its 8 lines. Most of them get a busy signal or time out, and we hold 5,000 calls in memory while we wait. With a channel, one producer sends the orders into a rendezvous channel, and 8 helper coroutines loop over it. Each order goes to exactly one helper, so at most 8 calls are in flight, and the producer just waits until a helper is free, which keeps memory flat. The helpers send their tickets into a second channel that one loop reads, and a separate coroutine closes that channel after all the helpers finish, so the loop can end. Because it all runs inside coroutineScope, one failed order cancels the producer and the other helpers, and the exception reaches the caller.

deeper.html:
actor { }, which older tutorials use to guard shared state with a channel of messages, is marked @ObsoleteCoroutinesApi: its KDoc says it will become obsolete when "complex actors" arrive. A plain coroutine looping over a channel you create does the same job without the warning, and the next lesson calls that confinement. BroadcastChannel was deprecated in 1.7, and its deprecation level was raised in 1.9. Use a SharedFlow from the last lesson for one-to-many.

The BUFFERED default of 64 comes from the JVM system property kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer. It is also the buffer that flowOn, buffer(), channelFlow and callbackFlow use unless you pass a size. When you size a pipeline for memory, count those hidden shelves too.

Channels also have trySend and tryReceive, which never suspend and return a ChannelResult. They are for code at the edge that can't suspend, like a listener callback, and trySendBlocking is the blocking variant for a plain thread that may wait. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 added ReceiveChannel.consumeTo(collection), which drains a channel into a collection.

The prime-sieve pipeline in the official channels guide is a fun read: each prime gets its own filtering coroutine, chained by channels, so the pipeline grows as it runs. It shows how cheap coroutines and channels are. It is a poor model for real programs, where a fixed number of stations with a known number of helpers is far easier to watch and to cancel.

This lesson is the first look at callbackFlow and the backpressure operators. Bridges and tests, in the Kotlin Flow in depth track, comes back to callbackFlow, and Buffering explains how buffer, conflate and flowOn merge their hidden channels into one.
